title: Elijah Taken Up; Elisha Receives His Spirit
summary: Elijah travels from Gilgal to Bethel to Jericho to the Jordan, and Elisha refuses to leave him. Elijah parts the Jordan with his cloak, Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit, and a chariot of fire separates them as Elijah goes up to heaven in a whirlwind. Elisha takes up the cloak, parts the Jordan himself, heals the spring at Jericho, and curses a crowd of jeering youths at Bethel.
story: This chapter is the hinge between the Elijah stories that dominated the end of 1 Kings and the Elisha stories that fill 2 Kings 2-8 and reach to chapter 13. Elijah had been told at Horeb to anoint Elisha as prophet in his place (1 Kings 19:16), and Elisha left his oxen and followed him (19:19-21). Now the handover is completed. The chapter answers a question that matters for the whole book: will the word of the LORD continue in Israel after its great prophet is gone? It does. The same power that parted the Jordan for Elijah parts it for Elisha, and the sons of the prophets recognize that Elijah's spirit rests on his successor.
historical:
The events fall around 852 BC, at the start of the reign of Jehoram (Joram) son of Ahab in Israel. The chapter does not date Elijah's departure precisely, and 2 Chronicles 21:12-15 records a letter from Elijah to Jehoram of Judah, which some interpreters take to mean that Elijah was still active a little later, or that the letter was written beforehand. The places named trace a route: Gilgal (probably not the Gilgal near Jericho but a town in the hill country north of Bethel, since they go down to Bethel from it), Bethel, Jericho, and across the Jordan to the east bank, near the region where Moses died and where Israel had first crossed into the land.

The sons of the prophets were communities of prophets gathered around a leader, found at Bethel, Jericho, and Gilgal in these chapters. Bethel was also the royal shrine of the northern kingdom, where Jeroboam had set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29), which helps explain the hostility Elisha meets there. Jericho had been rebuilt in Ahab's day at the cost of its builder's sons (1 Kings 16:34), under the curse Joshua had pronounced. The spring at Jericho that tradition identifies with Elisha's, a copious spring beside the ancient mound at Tell es-Sultan, still waters the oasis.
cultural:
A double portion was the inheritance of the firstborn son, who received twice the share of each of his brothers (Deuteronomy 21:17). Elisha is not asking to be twice as great as Elijah; he is asking to be recognized as Elijah's heir and successor. His cry, “My father, my father” (verse 12), fits that request, since prophets' disciples could call their master father. Tearing one's clothes was a sign of grief. The cloak, a prophet's mantle, stood for his office and authority; Elijah had thrown it over Elisha at his call (1 Kings 19:19), and now Elisha picks it up for good.

Salt had associations with purity and with covenant in Israel (Numbers 18:19 speaks of a covenant of salt), and a new bowl, not used for anything common, suits a sacred act. Shaving the head could be a mark of mourning or of certain vows, and baldness was open to mockery; whether Elisha was naturally bald or had a shaved head is not said. The words translated boys in verse 23 cover a wide range, from small children to young men, and the size of the crowd matters for understanding the scene.
literary: The first half of the chapter is built on a threefold pattern that slows the story and builds suspense. Three times Elijah asks Elisha to stay behind, three times Elisha swears he will not leave him, and at Bethel and Jericho the sons of the prophets ask whether he knows his master will be taken today, and he tells them to be silent. The crossing of the Jordan frames the ascension: Elijah strikes the water with his cloak and crosses, then Elisha strikes it with the same cloak and crosses back, repeating Israel's crossing under Joshua in reverse and then forward again. The chapter then gives two short signs of Elisha's authority that mirror each other: at Jericho a word brings healing and life, and at Bethel a word brings judgment. The narrator never describes the whirlwind itself in detail; Elisha's cry and his torn clothes carry the moment.

outline.t: Elisha refuses to leave Elijah at Gilgal, Bethel, and Jericho
The Jordan parted, the double portion, and the chariot of fire
Elisha takes up the cloak and the prophets search in vain

doctrines.note: The chapter's central gift is Elijah's spirit resting on Elisha (verse 15), which in context means the empowering of the LORD for prophetic work. The Spirit is not the possession of one great man; God passes his work on.
The word of the LORD does not die with the prophet. Elisha's first acts are introduced by the LORD's word (verse 21), and the narrator notes that it holds true to this day (verse 22).

Elijah does not die but is taken up, as Enoch was (Genesis 5:24). The Old Testament says little about life after death, but stories like this keep open the hope that God's servants are not simply lost to him.

words.note: Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's ruach, and the sons of the prophets see that Elijah's ruach rests on him. The word ranges from a gust of wind to the Spirit of the LORD, whom the prophets think may have carried Elijah off (verse 16). The range fits a chapter where a storm takes one prophet and the Spirit empowers another.

Adderet, a cloak or mantle, the outer garment that marked Elijah as a prophet. It is the same word used when Elijah threw his cloak over Elisha at his call (1 Kings 19:19). When Elisha picks it up and parts the Jordan with it, the cloak becomes the visible sign of a succession that is really the work of God.

Se'arah, whirlwind or storm. Elijah goes up in a se'arah, the same kind of storm from which the LORD later answers Job (Job 38:1). In the Old Testament a storm is often a sign of God's coming, and here it carries Elijah into his presence.

Rapha, to heal. It is the verb in the LORD's word at Jericho, “I have healed this water” (verse 21). The word is used for healing bodies, land, and water, and it recalls God's self-description as the LORD who heals (Exodus 15:26), spoken after bitter water was made sweet at Marah.

christ: Several threads in this chapter run toward the New Testament. Elijah is taken up to heaven, and his successor receives his spirit and carries on his work; Jesus ascends to heaven and his followers receive the Holy Spirit to continue his mission (Acts 1:8-11; 2:1-4). The pattern is thematic rather than predictive, and Luke seems to draw on it deliberately. Elisha's name means God is salvation, close in meaning to the name Joshua, of which Jesus is the Greek form, and Elisha's ministry of healing and feeding resembles Jesus' own. Elijah himself appears with Moses beside Jesus at the transfiguration (Mark 9:4). And the crossing of the Jordan, where Elisha begins his work, is where Jesus is baptized and the Spirit comes on him (Mark 1:9-10).

hard.q: How could a prophet of God curse children and have forty-two of them mauled by bears?
hard.a: This is one of the most troubling scenes in the Bible, and it deserves honest attention. Several features of the text bear on it. The Hebrew words for the youths can refer to young men as well as children, and the size of the crowd (at least forty-two were mauled) suggests a mob rather than a few small children. They came out of Bethel, the center of the calf worship that the prophets opposed, and their taunt, Go up, may mock the report of Elijah's ascension, telling the new prophet to disappear as his master had. On this reading the scene is a public rejection of the LORD's prophet at the moment his ministry begins, and the judgment echoes the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:22, which warns of wild animals sent among a rebellious people. Other interpreters, while accepting all of this, still find the punishment severe and note that the narrator reports it without comment. The text does not say that the youths were killed, only that they were mauled. What it presents is the LORD's judgment, not Elisha's personal revenge, since the curse is spoken in the LORD's name; readers differ on how much that eases the difficulty.

questions: Three times Elisha refused to leave Elijah. What does his persistence teach about following God when others tell you to stay behind?
Elisha asked for his master's spirit, not his cloak, and yet he used the cloak. How do outward signs relate to the reality they point to in your own faith?
The same prophet brings healing at Jericho and judgment at Bethel within a few verses. How do these two scenes together show what it means to carry the word of the LORD?
